content.overview: BNS s. 28 — Consent known to be given under fear or misconception.
content.study:
Introduction and meaning
Consent known to be given under fear or misconception. BNS restatement of IPC 90. Elements are substantially the same; cite the BNS number for offences on or after 1 July 2024. BNS restatement of IPC 90. Cite the BNS number for facts on or after 1 July 2024.
In student language: BNS s. 28 is the rule on “Consent known to be given under fear or misconception”. The section provides that a consent is not such a consent as is intended by any section of this Sanhita,–. Do not stop at the heading. An examiner awards marks for the ingredients, the explanations and the illustrations, not for writing the title alone.

Why this is asked
Criminal law arguments turn on statutory ingredients. BNS s. 28 exists so that “Consent known to be given under fear or misconception” has a closed legal test in Chapter III — General Exceptions. An authoritative analysis defines the concept, lists every ingredient, walks the statutory illustrations, states exceptions, and applies the test methodically to facts.
Chapter setting: When an act is not an offence: mistake, accident, infancy, unsoundness, consent, compulsion — and the right of private defence.

The provision in detail
28. A consent is not such a consent as is intended by any section of this Sanhita,–

(a) if the consent is given by a person under fear of injury, or under a misconception of fact, and if the person doing the act knows, or has reason to believe, that the consent was given in consequence of such fear or misconception; or

(b) if the consent is given by a person who, from unsoundness of mind, or intoxication, is unable to understand the nature and consequence of that to which he gives his consent; or

(c) unless the contrary appears from the context, if the consent is given by a person who is under twelve years of age

Essential ingredients

Step 1 — Identify the provision. The correct current-law cite is BNS s. 28 (Consent known to be given under fear or misconception), Chapter III — General Exceptions.
Step 2 — State the legal test in your own words, then list the ingredients:

Step 4 — Map each fact to an ingredient. Write “this fact proves ingredient (a)” or “this fact is missing, so the section is not made out”.
Step 5 — Conclude. If every essential ingredient is proved and no exception covers the case, BNS s. 28 applies. If any essential ingredient fails, say so and stop. Do not invent a different section to save the answer.

learningObjectives: Understand what constitutes vitiated or invalid consent under BNS s. 28.
Analyze the three grounds of vitiation: fear/misconception, unsoundness/intoxication, and infancy under twelve.
Examine the requirement of the doer's knowledge or reason to believe that consent was defective.
enhancement.definition: BNS s. 28 provides that a consent is not such a consent as is intended by any section of this Sanhita: (1) if given by a person under fear of injury, or under a misconception of fact, and if the person doing the act knows, or has reason to believe, that the consent was given in consequence of such fear or misconception; or (2) if given by a person who, from unsoundness of mind, or intoxication, is unable to understand the nature and consequence of that to which he gives consent; or (3) unless the contrary appears from the context, if given by a person who is under twelve years of age.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: Consent in criminal law requires a free, conscious, and voluntary exercise of mental will. Consent extracted by intimidation, induced by fraudulent misrepresentation of fact, or given by a person lacking cognitive capacity (infants, lunatics, intoxicated persons) is null in the eye of the penal law.
statutoryFramework: Chapter III — General Exceptions, BNS s. 28 (corresponding to IPC s. 90).
Vitiating Ground 1: Consent given under 'fear of injury' or 'misconception of fact', coupled with the doer's knowledge or reason to believe.
Vitiating Ground 2: Consent given by a person of unsound mind or intoxicated person unable to understand nature and consequence.
Vitiating Ground 3: Consent given by a child under twelve years of age.
Scope: Negative definition — applies across the entire Sanhita wherever consent is pleaded as a defence.
essentialIngredients: Consent was given by the victim.
The consent suffered from one of the statutory defects: fear of injury, misconception of fact, unsoundness, intoxication, or under twelve years of age.
In cases of fear or misconception, the doer knew or had reason to believe the consent was so induced.
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 28 does not define consent positively; it defines what is NOT valid consent. It establishes that submission is not consent. A consent given at knifepoint is given under fear of injury and is legally void. A misconception of fact must be a mistake regarding a fundamental factual element, not a mere promise regarding future uncertain events (unless made with fraudulent intent from inception). If the doer is unaware of the misconception and has no reason to suspect it, the doer is not penalized under this limb. For children under twelve and persons with severe cognitive impairment, incapacity to consent is statutory and absolute.
examples: Teaching example (Fear of injury): An armed gang surrounds a homeowner and demands jewelry. The homeowner hands it over. The gang cannot plead consent under s. 25 because consent was given under fear of injury.

Teaching example (Misconception of fact): A fraudulent quack represents that drinking acid is holy nectar that cures fever. The victim drinks it and dies. Consent was given under misconception of fact known to the quack; s. 28 invalidates consent.
distinctions: Consent vs Submission: Mere passive submission out of fear or helplessness does not amount to legal consent.
Misconception of fact vs Subsequent breach of promise: Misconception must exist at the time of giving consent regarding an existing fact, not a mere future breach of promise made in good faith.

Capacity under s. 28 (twelve years) vs s. 25 (eighteen years): Section 28 sets twelve as the general baseline below which no consent is valid; Section 25 specifically requires eighteen for taking risk of bodily harm in sports.
problemApplication: Issue: Whether consent obtained through a fraudulent misrepresentation of identity or medical qualifications is valid under BNS s. 28.
Rule: Under s. 28, consent given under a misconception of fact known to the doer is void.
Application: Check whether the accused knew the victim was consenting under a false belief regarding his qualifications or identity. If proved, the consent is legally non-existent.
Conclusion: The defence of consent fails by virtue of s. 28.
